tracks.title: The engine needs a midwife
tracks.text: Lesson seven point four — the deploy kit. A sub-lesson, under wbx. The engine needs a midwife. Here's the thing about every wbx engine verb… they all assume something is already running. Status talks to a Nexus. Dock needs one to dock into. [curious] But deploy is the one verb that has no engine to call — because its whole job is to make the engine exist. It is the bootstrap verb. Native only. There's no wasm build of it… because a wasm verb needs a runtime to run inside, and at deploy time… there isn't one yet. The status quo answers this with a zoo — a yaml file for the orchestrator, a second tool for the cloud, a secrets product wired to both, and a deploy script that complains the moment anything already exists. This lesson is the layer under one magic line. What file got written… what converged… where the secrets went… and what to type when it breaks.

tracks.title: The definition
tracks.text: The definition. The deploy kit is the bootstrap family inside wbx. One org file — deployment dot org. One converge verb set — init, validate, apply, status, logs, down, doctor, and secrets. And one provider seam. Together they stand an engine up from nothing… local or cloud… from a single declaration. And here's a detail that matters. The kit is compiled into the wbx binary. It ships inside the same static executable as every other verb. The deploy-kit directory on disk holds only its assets — example deployments, provider recipes, a storage example. [excited] You don't install the kit. You already have it… the moment you have wbx.

tracks.title: The whole config, annotated
tracks.text: The whole config, annotated. Let me read you the entire declaration — and I mean entire. Running deploy init local scaffolds exactly this. Line one, a title — Workbooks deployment. Line two — deploy target, local. Line three — deploy app, workbooks. Line four — deploy port, four thousand. Then a comment, reminding you that secrets are named here but set elsewhere. Then deploy secrets — openrouter A P I key. And a closing comment — that the image defaults to the published runtime, and the W B image variable can override it. That's five real lines and two comments. Nothing hidden. Now, every key has a fallback and a default — let me give you the ones to hold onto. Target decides where it runs, and defaults to local — that single value is the local-versus-cloud switch. App names the engine, default workbooks. Port defaults to four thousand. And image — this is the one to memorize — resolves on a ladder. The W B image environment variable beats the file… the file beats the built-in default of the published runtime image. [curious] That ladder is how you pin a specific build in C I, or test a local image… without ever editing the artifact.

tracks.title: The converge loop
tracks.text: The converge loop. The verb set is the same manners every wbx family uses — init to scaffold, validate to check, apply to make it so, then status, logs, and down to live with it. Three are worth dwelling on. First, init. On a terminal — a human — it shows a two-option picker. Local, a container on this machine, cloud-identical… versus cloud, fly dot I O, under your own account. But piped, or run by an agent, it skips the prompt and takes the safe default — local. Second, validate. It loads the file, checks that a cloud target has a resolvable recipe, and warns — but does not fail — on secrets that are declared but unset. Third, apply. Same checks… but apply hard-fails on missing secrets. Validate tells you what's wrong. Apply refuses to ship something half-configured. Now picture the flow as a graph. At the top, one box — deployment dot org, the single declaration. An arrow down to validate. If that's clean, an arrow to apply. And here apply forks — on the one value in the file. If target is local… it drives the built-in container seam — docker, podman, or krunvm. If target is some other place… it hands off to that provider's recipe — a bootstrap script. Both paths arrive at the same node — engine up. And from there, status, logs, and down loop, each dispatching on that same target. There's one more arrow — a dotted one — looping from down all the way back to apply. [curious] That dotted line is the whole idea. Apply is a converge, not a script. Re-run it and it re-pulls the image, replaces the container, re-stages the secrets… and never complains that anything already exists.

tracks.title: Local, step by step
tracks.text: Local, step by step. With target set to local, apply finds a container engine in automation-friendliness order — docker, then podman, then krunvm — the first whose version command spawns. On docker, it amounts to a handful of lines. First, docker pull — fetch the runtime image. Second, docker remove, force, workbooks — this is the idempotent part, removing any old container so there's never a name conflict. Third, docker run — detached, named workbooks, publishing port four thousand, with the web flag on, mounting two volumes, and pointing at the secrets env-file. Two volumes carry the durable state. Slash data holds the registry database, so your deployed workbooks survive a restart. And slash disco is the discovery seam. Picture the handshake as a short sequence. Apply calls docker — pull, remove, run. Docker starts the container. The container writes a file — runtime dot json — into slash disco, carrying the scheme, the port, and the token. Apply prints… engine up… try wb rt status. And then status reads that same runtime dot json and just connects — no U R L to type. [excited] That's why local needs no configuration to talk to itself — discovery is a file on disk. For a remote engine, you'd instead set the engine U R L, and the engine token if it's locked. More on that token next.

tracks.title: Names in the file, values in the vault
tracks.text: Names in the file… values in the vault. The artifact says what it needs. It never holds what it needs. Deploy secrets, openrouter A P I key — that's a declaration of a name. The value lives in a file called secrets dot env, in your app directory, written with permissions six-oh-oh — owner read-write only. Let me read you the round trip. You run deploy secrets set, openrouter key equals, your value. It replies — staged one secret… applied on the next apply. Now if you run apply with a name still missing, it stops cold — error, declared secrets unset, openrouter A P I key… run secrets set, or export them, first. Two delivery paths, one declaration. Locally, the kit passes the secrets file as an env-file to the container. In the cloud, it stages each value through the provider's set-secrets hook. Either way, values travel as environment at start time… and never enter deployment dot org or the image. Picture that as a flow. On the left, the declared name. It flows to the value — the secrets file, or an exported variable. From there, two arrows — one to the local env-file path, one to the cloud hook — and both land at the same place, the container's environment at start time. And then two more arrows, fat and red, pointing at the artifact and the image, each labeled… never. [curious] That's the whole promise — nothing on the value side ever reaches the file or the image. Now, there's one secret the kit generates for you. On the first cloud apply, it mints a two-hundred-fifty-six-bit random token from the operating system's randomness, persists it as the public bearer in the secrets file, and prints once — control plane locked… bearer token generated… export the engine token to talk to it. It never rotates… on purpose. Rotation would four-oh-one every live client mid-flight. And the runtime enforces the other half — once that bearer is set, the engine is a locked deploy. No token… four-oh-one… no fallback. Lose the printed token? You recover it from the secrets file. Same value… sitting where it always was.

tracks.title: Same file, different value
tracks.text: Same file… different value. Moving the engine to the cloud is editing one property — deploy target, fly. No new tool. No second config language. On apply, the bundled fly recipe converges — creating only what's missing. It ensures the fly app exists. It stages secrets additively. It creates a one-gigabyte volume called wbdata if it's absent. And it synthesizes a small fly config in a temp directory. Let me read you that config. App — my workbooks engine. Primary region — sjc. A build section, pointing image at the published runtime. A mounts section — source wbdata, destination slash data. And an H T T P service — internal port four thousand, force https true, and two lines that matter most — auto stop machines, stop… and minimum machines running, zero. [curious] That last pair is scale-to-zero by default. The engine sleeps when nobody's talking, and wakes on the next request. And your workbooks survive the sleep, because the registry database lives on the slash data volume — litestream replicates it. The public U R L comes back as your app, dot fly dot dev. And then, if the file declared deploy toolkits, the kit asks the recipe for that U R L and pushes each toolkit. [excited] The kit ships the engine and its toolkits, in one apply. And notice — the local docker run and this fly config express the same engine contract. A container, a port, a volume, secrets as environment. That sameness… is the provider-agnostic claim, made concrete.

tracks.title: Five hooks and a spine
tracks.text: Five hooks and a spine. A provider here is not a plugin S D K — it's a shell file. Local is the built-in container seam. Anything else is a recipe — a bootstrap script that sources a neutral spine and fills five hooks, plus a lifecycle trio. Fly is just the one that ships bundled — explicitly a personal preference, not a privileged path. Let me walk the five hooks and what fly does for each. First — ensure app — make the app exist — fly creates it if missing. Second — set secrets — stage the declared values — fly stages them additively. Third — attach volume — give it durable storage — fly makes the one-gigabyte volume if it's absent. Fourth — deploy image — run the engine container — fly synthesizes its config and deploys by reference. Fifth — public url — where to reach it — fly returns your app dot fly dot dev. And the lifecycle trio — down, status, logs — destroy the app, read machine state, tail the logs. The verdict of that table — five hooks plus three, and a provider is done. The spine hands the recipe a clean environment, carrying only the path, the home directory, the deploy variables, and the staged secrets — so credentials reach the hook without ever touching the C L I's own process environment. [excited] So adding A W S, or Render, or your own server, is dropping a bootstrap script — no recompile. There is no ephemeral-sandbox half to implement — it's one container, with wasm inside. Authoring a full provider is its own deep dive — the recipes lesson. This page stays at the contract.

tracks.title: When it doesn't converge
tracks.text: When it doesn't converge. Deploy doctor is the debugging entry point. Picture its report as three little sections. First — engines — a checklist. Docker, a checkmark, version present. Podman, a cross, not found. Krunvm, a cross, not found. Fly, a checkmark. Second — recipes — it lists fly, resolved from the copy embedded in the binary. Third — secrets — a cross, missing, openrouter A P I key. One screen… that tells you why apply can't proceed. Three failures are canonical, and each names its own fix. No engine at all — install one, or use deploy init cloud. Image pull fails — the hint asks, is it published… override with W B image — because the default image is a published reference, and a private build needs the override. Missing secrets — the exact bail, declared secrets unset… run secrets set, or export them. And these tie back to the wbx exit codes. A verb that can't reach the engine exits three… and its hint names deploy local. [curious] The loop closes right back here — at the verb that brings the engine up.

tracks.title: Edges, named
tracks.text: Edges, named — because a bootstrap tool that hides its limits is the worst kind. First — krunvm can't take the secrets env-file yet. Docker and podman deliver it… krunvm can't. So if a deployment declares secrets and only krunvm is present, apply bails — use docker or podman, or a cloud provider. A real gap. Second — one cloud recipe ships today. Fly is bundled. Everything else is a bootstrap script someone writes. The seam is open… the shelf is short. Third — cloud needs flyctl and your own account. The recipe exits with an install link if flyctl isn't on the path, and the app lands under your fly account, not ours. Fourth — the file is deployment dot org, in the current directory. The verb reads exactly that path — no file argument. The richer example files carry a fuller axis set — tenancy, storage, auth — but those are read by the engine-side backend, not by this verb. They still ride to the engine… as environment… just not yet as first-class keys. And fifth — the bearer never rotates… and that's a feature. Rotation would four-oh-one every live client. The kit chooses stability, and stores the one token at six-oh-oh.

tracks.title: Questions people actually ask
tracks.text: Quick fire. [curious] Do I need Docker? Any one of docker, podman, or krunvm covers local — the kit picks the first it finds. Or skip local and go straight to cloud. Where exactly do my secrets live? In a file called secrets dot env, in your app directory, at permissions six-oh-oh. List shows names only… never values. Can I re-run apply safely? Yes — that's the whole model. It converges — re-pulls, replaces the container, re-stages secrets, without complaining. The one thing it will not touch… is the bearer. Re-applying never rotates it. How do I point wbx at the deployed engine? Locally it's automatic — the container writes runtime dot json and the C L I reads it. For a remote engine, set the engine U R L, plus the engine token if it's locked. A W S, Render, my own server? Write a bootstrap script, fill the five hooks and the trio, and set the target. No recompile. And — is wb deploy how Workbooks itself ships? [chuckles] No. This is the users' tool. Workbooks' own platform releases ship through C I and a manual maintainer step. The kit runs the engine… it doesn't publish it.

tracks.title: Back up to wbx
tracks.text: So that's the deploy kit. One org file declares the engine. One converge verb set stands it up. And where it runs — your laptop or a cloud account — is a value in the file, not a different tool. Secrets declared by name… never baked in. [curious] If any of it felt like it needed more ground under it, the way back up is short. This is a sub-lesson under wbx — lesson seven — the command line, where the verb manners and the exit codes live. Start there. And then follow the engine this verb brings to life… the Nexus.
